newsitem.title: USA: Dornan vows to fight recount that confirmed his loss.
newsitem.headline: Dornan vows to fight recount that confirmed his loss.

text.p: Orange County election officials on Friday said a recount of ballots has confirmed the defeat of veteran arch-conservative Republican Representative Robert Dornan to Democrat Loretta Sanchez.
A recount of ballots from the Nov. 5 election showed that Sanchez beat Dornan by 979 votes. Sanchez won with 48,056 versus Dornan's 47,077, election officials said.
In a statement issued Friday, Sanchez, 36, called on Dornan to accept the results.
"It is time for Mr. Dornan to accept the will of the people and move on," Sanchez said. "The people of the district have spoken. The verdict has been confirmed."
But Dornan attorney Michael Schroeder said they intended to contest the results in state Superior Court next week.
"We've been able to develop more than adequate evidence of voter fraud and improper conduct from the recount to file an election contest to have to election overturned," Schroeder said late Friday.
Dornan, a feisty Republican known as "B-1-Bob" because of his strong support for the military, had called for the recount after his narrow defeat to Sanchez in the election.
The November results showed Dornan lost by 984 votes, but Dornan, 63, and his supporters alleged non-citizens voted and that ballot boxes were not correctly sealed after the polls.

Schroeder asserted Friday that from 2,500 to 3,500 ballots from the November election should be thrown out because of voting irregularities allegedly uncovered during the recount. He said as many 1,000 non-citizens and felons had voted.
But Orange County Registrar of Voters Rosalyn Lever said Friday that there was "no sign of any (voting) irregularities" from the recount. "There were no surprises," she said.

Sanchez spokesman John Shallman said that "not a single shred of evidence" was found during the recount of irregularities. He accused Dornan of spreading allegations of voter fraud "to capture headlines and keep the money flowing."
Dornan, a former Air Force pilot, gained a reputation for strong opposition to abortion, communism, equal rights for homosexuals and gun control during his 18 years in Congress.
Sanchez, a financial analyst who had never held elected office, campaigned as a moderate while painting Dornan as an extremist out of step with the needs of his largely working-class constituents.
